title: One Compromised Login Exposed Millions of California Students’ Records
description: Intruders used compromised credentials to access an Educational Testing Service (ETS) SFTP server, copying records of California public school students dating back to 2006. The breach was discovered on September 25, 2026, but unauthorized access occurred intermittently from May 22 to September 18, 2026. The exposed data includes personal information such as student names, birth dates, addresses, school details, and sensitive educational data, but excludes Social Security numbers, passwords, financial information, and parent/guardian data. ETS disabled the compromised account and took the SFTP site offline, working on a replacement with stronger security. Notifications and identity protection services are being provided to affected individuals. The exact method of credential compromise and attacker identity remain unknown.
aiSummary: This incident involved unauthorized access to an ETS SFTP server using compromised login credentials. The attackers accessed and copied files containing detailed information on California public school students, including those currently enrolled and former students dating back to 2006. The data set includes personally identifiable information and sensitive educational details but does not contain Social Security numbers or financial data. The breach was active from late May through mid-September 2026 before detection. ETS responded by disabling the compromised account, taking the site offline, and initiating development of a more secure replacement system. Law enforcement and cybersecurity experts were engaged, and no evidence of public data disclosure has been found to date. Notifications and free identity protection services are being offered to affected students.
aiImpact: The breach exposed personal and sensitive educational information of millions of California public school students, including current and former students over a 20-year span. While Social Security numbers and financial data were not compromised, the exposed data could facilitate identity theft, privacy violations, and targeted phishing or social engineering attacks. The scale of the breach is significant given California's large student population, potentially affecting over 5.7 million students. The incident also disrupted ETS operations, including suspension of enrollment data processing and some testing activities.
